sections.title: June Crew Council Minutes
sections.text:
The Grand Canyon monthly meeting was a comprehensive planning session focused on trip logistics, group dynamics, safety, training, and communication for the upcoming winter river expedition. Brian Cain led the meeting, starting with a historical quote from John Wesley Powell to set the tone for adventure and uncertainty, but emphasized that the group would be well-prepared by the time of launch.

The group discussed the current roster, noting that while the permit allows for up to 16 people, not all are fully committed yet. Brian stressed the importance of team cohesion and being selective about adding new members, given the challenging nature of the trip. The group reviewed the Google Drive folder containing planning resources, including a master spreadsheet with river segments, campsites, rapids (rated on the Grand Canyon’s unique 1-9 scale), and GPX files for navigation.

A major focus was the itinerary: the trip launches from Lee’s Ferry on December 28, with a mandatory ranger check-in the day before. The group must average 17.6 miles per day to reach key milestones, particularly Cremation Camp near Phantom Ranch, where a crew swap and mule-supported gear transfer are planned. The limited daylight in late December (about 9 hours, with even less sun at the canyon bottom) was highlighted as a significant challenge, making efficiency and early starts critical. The group discussed the pace required, referencing past trips and the need to balance rowing speed with time for scouting rapids and camp setup.

Takeout options were debated: Phantom Ranch (with a strenuous 5,000-foot hike out), Diamond Creek, and Pierce Ferry. The consensus leaned toward taking out at Diamond Creek to allow for a layover day and a less rushed experience, rather than pushing through the less scenic, flat-water stretch to Pierce Ferry. The group valued having buffer days for side hikes (like Havasu), rest, and contingency in case of delays due to weather or mishaps.

Logistics for travel to and from the river were reviewed, including airport options (Flagstaff, Las Vegas, St. George), car rentals, and outfitter shuttles. The group discussed the need for efficient meal planning (possibly focusing on big dinners and simple breakfasts), gear redundancies (extra shoes, chairs, walkie-talkies), and the importance of a comprehensive gear list. There was also discussion about filming the trip, with questions about camera mounts and safety.

Training was emphasized as essential, with recommendations for cardio, core strength, and endurance to handle consecutive long rowing days and the strenuous hike out for those exiting at Phantom Ranch. Injury prevention and gradual buildup were stressed, and the group encouraged sharing training plans and using Strava for motivation. Swiftwater rescue courses and online safety resources were recommended.

For communication, the group agreed to transition from text to Telegram for better organization, with the possibility of using an AI chatbot for FAQs. A practice trip to Westwater Canyon was proposed for the fall as a tune-up, with a poll to be conducted for scheduling. The meeting concluded with reminders to crowdsource future agenda topics, excitement for the adventure, and a lighthearted discussion about team commitment and the possibility of applying for a documentary with TGR.

sections.title: July 20th Crew Council Minutes
sections.text:
The meeting discussed logistics for an upcoming Grand Canyon trip, focusing on reaching Phantom Ranch and deciding between Diamond Creek and Pierce Ferry for the final takeout. The group aims to leave Lee's Ferry on Sunday, with options to reach Phantom Ranch by Saturday or Sunday, averaging 14.7 miles per day. For the lower section, they considered reaching Diamond Creek on Wednesday, Friday, or Saturday, with potential side hikes to Havasu Canyon. The group debated the pros and cons of reaching Pierce Ferry, including the impact on travel plans and the need for additional resupply. A tentative plan was to reach Diamond Creek on Saturday and Pierce Ferry on Monday. The team discussed logistics for their Grand Canyon trip, confirming 11 participants and planning to use four boats with two to three people per boat. They debated whether to end at Phantom Ranch or Pierce Ferry, opting for Pierce Ferry on Sunday to allow for more side hikes and layover days. They also considered alternative rivers like the Snake due to low flows in Westwater Canyon. Brian Cain emphasized the importance of rowing practice and shared resources for navigating the rapids. Concerns about potential flash flooding due to a Super El Nino event were raised, but reassurances were given based on weather monitoring.

Grand Canyon | Monthly Meeting — August 3, 2026
 
Overview
 
The group discussed their upcoming Grand Canyon river trip, focusing on logistics and gear. They plan to cover 14.7 miles per day on the upper section and 10.6 miles per day on the lower section, aiming for a relaxed pace. They will leave from Diamond Creek and takeout at Phantom Ranch. Brian Cain shared a detailed gear list and suggested appointing team members to manage specific tasks like food and gear setup. They also discussed the importance of proper gear, including a hot tent, and the potential for themed meals and cocktails. The next meeting will finalize gear and meal plans. The group discussed logistics for an upcoming trip to the Grand Canyon, emphasizing the importance of finalizing gear lists by August 15th. They planned to meet on August 17th to address gear questions and finalize rental needs. Brian Cain suggested moving the September 7th meeting to August 31st. They also discussed the need for a hunting tent and other equipment, with some members offering to source items locally. Complete hydraulics and hazard-recognition progression through advanced rowing material.
Complete ferrying, eddies, oar management, downstream ferry, and aggressive-move modules.
Review river signals/communication and boat order/spacing.
Review defensive swimming, rescue hierarchy, and conditional rescue concepts.
Review choosing a throw bag plus Throw Bags 101 and 201.
Review Oar Boat Flipping 101–301; understand roles before hands-on practice.
Complete Big Three knots, advanced knots, boat-based anchors, and land-based anchors.
Complete pin/wrap kit, pin management, MA safety, 3:1, transport hitch, and vector pull.
Review evacuation example and CPR for drowning.
Review raft repair in the field before final gear shakedown.

sections.title: Hands-on skills to practice as a group
rows: Video knowledge is not enough; build accuracy, communication, and safe rope handling.
Everyone should know how to behave as a swimmer and how the crew will recover swimmers.
Clarifies roles and builds confidence before an actual flip.
Make sure everyone understands safe deployment and entanglement concerns.
Core knots should be automatic under stress.
Useful for boat recovery and rescue systems.
Foundation for shore-based rescue and mechanical advantage.
Lay out entire kit and assign locations
Everyone involved should know what is in the kit and where each component lives.
Practice system construction, communication, redirects, and safety zones.
Non-rescuers still need to understand where not to stand and how to assist safely.
A multi-boat Grand Canyon trip depends on spacing, visibility, and clear signals.
Practice concise line descriptions, hazards, and downstream contingencies.
Know where repair supplies are and how to handle common field damage.
Everyone should know basic messaging, SOS escalation, and the group's communication plan.
Crew should know where medical gear is stored and how it is organized.

sections.title: Grand Canyon–specific education
rows: Review major hazards, scout locations, and likely lines before launch.
Grand Canyon boat spacing / downstream ferry concepts
Discuss how long wave trains, eddies, and current differentials affect a multi-boat group.
Recognition, prevention, rewarming, wet-gear response, and winter layering expectations.
Discuss how weather may alter launch time, mileage, camps, layovers, and side hikes.
Warning signs, weather awareness, safe hiking decisions, and turnaround criteria.
Buddy expectations, solo time at camp, check-in plans, and what happens if a party is overdue.
Who communicates, what information is relayed, and how the group supports an evacuation.
Practice reporting river mile/location, critical vs. stable, trauma vs. medical, and private vs. commercial.
Grand Canyon tides / dam release fluctuations
Understand rising/falling water at camps and how flow timing may affect decisions.
Review current regulations and participant responsibilities before launch.
Review access restrictions and expectations around tribal lands and Diamond Creek.
Discuss what happens if road access is delayed or compromised.

sections.title: Tabletop / emergency scenarios
rows: Who does what in the first 60 seconds?
How do we manage people, boat spacing, and recovery?
Who leads, who assists, and where are the danger zones?
Serious injury on a side hike
How do we assess, communicate location, and decide on evacuation?
How do we recognize it and rewarm without creating more risk?
What is the pre-agreed regrouping / communication plan?
What information triggers a turnaround or no-go decision?
What exact information gets sent and who communicates?
What is the backup communication plan?
Who decides, and how do we protect schedule flexibility and morale?
